timeline: You probably assume every stone pillar in the 1530 AD Veerabhadra temple carries weight, but one hangs entirely in the air.
Built during the reign of King Achyuta Deva Raya, seventy granite columns fill this grand hall.
Yet a single pillar near the corner stays dislodged from the stone floor beneath it.
A clear gap separates the stone base from the rocky ground.
Devotees routinely slide a thin cotton cloth completely underneath to test the physical anomaly.
The fabric passes freely from one side to the other without obstruction.
Visitors often inspect the pillar to understand how medieval builders achieved this balance.
They feared moving it might cause the entire hall overhead to collapse.
Modern architects remain equally baffled by how medieval builders achieved this balance.
Some suggest it was left slightly displaced intentionally during construction.
Others argue centuries of seismic settling shifted the load entirely onto surrounding supports.
Two brothers named Virupanna and Viranna funded this architectural marvel under King Achyuta.
Today, millions visit the site to witness gravity seemingly defied by ancient stone.
Yet nobody can explain how a heavy pillar hangs without touching the floor.
You probably assume every stone pillar in the 1530 AD Veerabhadra temple carries weight, but one hangs entirely in the air.
